frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial fishing, recreational boating) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon if it offers a reliable, low-cost emergency alert solution that is easy to carry and integrates with existing navigation gear.
T1.who_benefits: Individual hikers, campers, and outdoor recreationists who value safety and need a device that complements their existing gear.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A reliable distress beacon reduces perceived risk and provides peace of mind, making the purchase decision more appealing than relying solely on smartphones or existing communication methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can price the beacon at a modest premium (e.g., $150-200) and sell it through outdoor retailers and online channels, capturing margin on each unit while leveraging existing distribution.
assumptions: Outdoor recreationists have sufficient disposable income to purchase a $150-200 device.
They trust and will use the 406 MHz distress signal for emergency situations.
Existing communication methods (e.g., cell phones, satellite phones) are not always reliable in remote areas.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $150-200.
Sales of the beacon will be positively correlated with outdoor recreation participation rates in a region.
Adoption will be higher when the beacon is bundled with a compatible GPS device or navigation app.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon if it offers a reliable, low-cost emergency alert solution that is easy to carry and integrates with existing navigation gear.

T2.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons if they can be integrated into existing SAR protocols and provide reliable, standardized signals that can be detected across jurisdictions.
T2.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, coast guards, and emergency response teams that need reliable, interoperable distress signals to locate and assist remote individuals.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A standardized distress beacon reduces the time and cost of identifying and responding to emergencies, and the ability to detect signals across borders can improve international coordination.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon to governments and SAR agencies at a higher price point (e.g., $300-500) and offer service contracts for maintenance and data sharing, generating recurring revenue.
assumptions: SAR agencies have budget to acquire and maintain new equipment.
Interoperability standards exist or can be established for 406 MHz signals.
Current distress signal methods are insufficient for remote or international incidents.
predictions: SAR agencies will express interest in purchasing 406 MHz beacons for operational use.
Adoption will be higher in regions with high outdoor recreation density and multiple SAR jurisdictions.
Sales will be driven by pilot programs or government procurement contracts.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, low-cost emergency solution for remote travel.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, climbers) who need a lightweight, easy-to-use distress device.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users already carry survival gear and are willing to invest in safety equipment that reduces risk and improves rescue chances.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers at a modest price point, capturing margin through volume sales and brand association with safety-conscious outdoor recreation.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. were stable or growing in 2002.
Consumers are aware of the 406 MHz distress beacon technology and understand its benefits.
Price sensitivity is acceptable for this segment, with a price point under $200.
predictions: If ACR launches a consumer-focused outdoor beacon with a clear marketing message, at least 5% of surveyed outdoor recreationists will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation density (e.g., national parks, mountain states).
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, low-cost emergency solution for remote travel.

T2.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a standardized, reliable signal that can be detected across vast, remote areas, reducing response time.
T2.who_benefits: Emergency response agencies (e.g., FEMA, Coast Guard, state SAR teams) and search-and-rescue operators who need a consistent, interoperable distress signal.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These agencies already operate on standardized radio frequencies and are tasked with rapid response to life-threatening emergencies; a reliable, satellite-based distress beacon aligns with their operational needs.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons to government agencies and SAR contractors at a premium price, capturing value through volume contracts and long-term service agreements.
assumptions: Emergency response agencies have budget allocations for new safety equipment in 2002.
Interoperability between different agencies is a critical purchase criterion.
Price sensitivity is lower for government procurement compared to consumer markets.
predictions: If ACR offers a beacon marketed as a SAR-grade, at least 10% of surveyed emergency response agencies will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with high SAR activity (e.g., coastal states, mountain ranges).

arguments.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, paddlers) who travel in remote areas where other communication methods are unreliable.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These users already carry safety gear and are aware of the risk of isolation; a distress beacon that uses the established 406 MHz satellite network provides a credible emergency solution that can be used in life-threatening situations.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and potentially partner with outdoor brands for co‑branding, leveraging existing distribution channels.

The 406 MHz frequency is known and trusted for distress signaling by SAR.
Consumers will differentiate between a distress beacon and a general GPS tracker.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point above $300.
Purchase intent will be higher when the beacon is presented as a safety‑critical tool rather than a general GPS device.
Actual purchase conversion will be at least 10% of those indicating intent.

arguments.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, emergency services, and government agencies responsible for remote area response.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: SAR teams rely on standardized distress signals to locate victims; the 406 MHz frequency is the only global distress frequency, ensuring beacons can be detected across borders and oceans.

Government procurement cycles can be leveraged to secure large orders.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Legalization of 406 MHz PLBs in the US (2002) and increased media coverage of successful rescues create a perceived safety necessity; these users already carry emergency gear and are motivated by personal safety.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a premium-priced, easy-to-use distress beacon directly to consumers through outdoor retailers and online channels, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.

Consumers will prioritize safety over cost in a life-threatening situation.
Distribution channels (outdoor retailers, online) can reach the target audience.
predictions: A survey of outdoor recreation participants will show >50% would purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $200-300.
Sales of ACR’s existing PLB will increase if marketed as a consumer product.
Competitor entry will be limited by regulatory exclusivity and high cost of entry.

arguments.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a differentiated consumer distress beacon because they value safety in remote environments and are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides reliable distress signaling.
arguments.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who engage in activities where emergency response is limited.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Legalization of 406 MHz PLBs in the US (2002) and increased media coverage of successful rescues create a perceived safety necessity; these users already carry emergency gear and are motivated by personal safety.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a premium-priced, easy-to-use distress beacon directly to consumers through outdoor retailers and online channels, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Legalization and media coverage will sustain consumer awareness and demand.
Consumers will prioritize safety over cost in a life-threatening situation.
Distribution channels (outdoor retailers, online) can reach the target audience.
predictions: A survey of outdoor recreation participants will show >50% would purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $200-300.
Sales of ACR’s existing PLB will increase if marketed as a consumer product.
Competitor entry will be limited by regulatory exclusivity and high cost of entry.

arguments.claim: Commercial marine operators and personal safety professionals will adopt a differentiated consumer distress beacon because they need a reliable, easy-to-use emergency signaling device for remote operations and search-and-rescue.
arguments.who_benefits: Commercial marine operators (yachts, cruise ships), personal safety professionals (offshore oil/gas, diving), and search-and-rescue agencies that require a standardized distress beacon.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Legalization of 406 MHz PLBs and the need for a reliable, compliant distress beacon for remote operations; these users already operate in high-risk environments and are willing to invest in safety equipment.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a professional-grade, easy-to-deploy distress beacon through marine distributors and safety equipment retailers, capturing higher margins than consumer sales and leveraging existing B2B relationships.
assumptions: Commercial operators prioritize regulatory compliance and safety over cost.
Professional users will adopt a device that reduces training requirements and improves operational efficiency.
Distribution channels (marine distributors, safety equipment retailers) can reach the target audience.
predictions: A survey of marine operators and safety professionals will show >40% would purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $500-800.
Sales of ACR’s existing PLB will increase if marketed as a professional safety product.
Competitor entry will be limited by regulatory exclusivity and high cost of entry.

arguments.quote: The 406 MHz PLB is primarily intended to provide a distress and alerting capacity for use by the general public in life threatening situations in a remote environment after all other means of notifying SAR responders (e.g., telephone, radio) have been exhausted.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show that outdoor recreation enthusiasts specifically would adopt the device, nor that they would pay a premium price.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Outdoor Recreation PLB
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from outdoor recreation communities (hikers, paddlers, climbers) via outdoor forums and social media. They are shown two product descriptions: (1) Safety‑focused: "A 406 MHz PLB that provides emergency distress signaling in remote environments, saving lives and ensuring SAR response." (2) Status‑focused: "A 406 MHz PLB that signals preparedness and expertise, allowing you to demonstrate your commitment to safety and your place in the outdoor community." Participants are asked: "Which product would you be more likely to purchase?" and "What is the maximum price you would pay?" The survey also collects demographic data (age, gender, years of outdoor activity) and self‑reported importance of safety versus status.
X1.sample: 300 participants, balanced across age and gender, recruited from outdoor forums and social media groups with high activity levels.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants choosing the safety‑focused product over the status‑focused product. Secondary outcomes: average price willingness (EUR) for each product, and self‑reported importance of safety versus status.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety‑focused product will be chosen by ≥60% of participants, and price willingness for safety product will be ≥EUR300.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status‑focused product will be chosen by ≥60% of participants, and price willingness for status product will be ≥EUR500.

X1.decision_rule: If safety‑focused product choice ≥60% AND safety price willingness ≥EUR300, proceed with safety‑focused consumer proposition. If status‑focused product choice ≥60% AND status price willingness ≥EUR500, proceed with status‑focused consumer proposition. If neither condition met, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand for a 406 MHz distress beacon. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

If the survey shows ≥60% preference for the safety‑focused product and willingness to pay ≥€300, proceed with a limited launch targeting outdoor recreation enthusiasts. Otherwise, maintain current B2B/B2G focus and explore licensing the 406 MHz‑
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who engage in activities with inherent risk of isolation and who value safety as a core activity requirement.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a safety necessity that increases survival probability in remote environments, sold through outdoor retailer and online channels at a price point justifying premium over basic PLBs.
final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week budget of €15,000 to measure willingness to purchase and choice between safety‑focused and status‑focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: Demand for a consumer distress beacon among outdoor recreation enthusiasts is unknown; evidence of actual purchase behavior or willingness to pay is lacking. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows <60% preference for the safety‑focused product or willingness to pay <€300, the recommendation would shift to maintain the current B2B/B2G focus and explore licensing the technology to third parties.
If additional independent market data from 2002 showed strong consumer adoption of 406 MHz PLBs, the recommendation would shift toward a full consumer launch.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Investment decision must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching the target market.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home‑garden, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (status quo).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B dealer model for farm and industrial equipment.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a new subsidiary or spin‑out to create a consumer brand, leveraging Deere’s engineering but operating independently of the core business.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing small‑garden households need a machine that can mow, till, and pull small implements; a tractor that is easy to use and maintain is more attractive than a specialized tool.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its brand and engineering to command a premium price for a consumer‑friendly product.
assumptions: Small‑garden households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to purchase a lawn and garden tractor.
Deere’s dealer network can reach these households and provide adequate service.
The tractor’s versatility justifies the price point.
predictions: If Deere introduces a consumer‑focused lawn and garden tractor, sales through existing dealers will increase relative to a control group.
Customer surveys will rank the tractor’s versatility and ease of use as primary purchase drivers.

X1.sample: 200 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region. Participants are randomly assigned to see either Description A or Description B.

Participants view a product description of a John Deere lawn and garden tractor (1962 model) and are asked: "Which benefit would motivate you to purchase this tractor?" X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25‑65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region.
X1.measure: Proportion of participants selecting Convenience/Time Savings as primary motivation (T1) vs. Status/Prestige (T2). Secondary measure: average WTP in dollars.

prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of participants will select Status/Prestige as primary motivation, and average WTP will be above $1,000.

final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25‑65, to measure motivation and willingness to pay.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a John Deere lawn and garden tractor (1962 model) emphasizing either status/modern convenience (T1) or affordability/reliable power (T2). They are asked: "Which benefit would motivate you to purchase this tractor?" (status/modern convenience vs. affordability/reliable power). They also rate willingness to pay on a 7‑point scale. X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who select status/modern convenience as the primary benefit (T1) vs. affordability/reliable power (T2). Secondary: average willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 55% of participants will select status/modern convenience as the primary benefit, and average WTP will be above $1,500.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 55% of participants will select affordability/reliable power as the primary benefit, and average WTP will be below $1,500.

X1.decision_rule: If the observed proportion selecting status/modern convenience ≥ 55% AND average WTP ≥ $1,500, then T1 is supported. If the observed proportion selecting affordability/reliable power ≥ 55% AND average WTP ≥ $1,500, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of homeowner demand for status/modern convenience versus affordability/reliable power in 1962.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a John Deere lawn and garden tractor (1962 model) emphasizing either status/modern convenience (T1) or affordability/reliable power (T2). They are asked: "Which benefit would motivate you to purchase this tractor?" (status/modern convenience vs. affordability/reliable power). They also rate willingness to pay on a 7‑point scale. The survey is run
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who select status/modern convenience as the primary benefit (T1) vs. affordability/reliable power (T2). Secondary: average willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 55% of participants will select status/modern convenience as the primary benefit, and average WTP will be above $1,500.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 55% of participants will select affordability/reliable power as the primary benefit, and average WTP will be below $1,500.

arguments.decision_rule: If the observed proportion selecting status/modern convenience ≥ 55% AND average WTP ≥ $1,500, then T1 is supported. If the observed proportion selecting affordability/reliable power ≥ 55% AND average WTP ≥ $1,500, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (Test X1) to validate demand for status/modern convenience versus affordability/reliable power before committing resources.
